GPS and maps

Remember where the day took you.

Some trips stay in one place. Others unfold across miles of river, shoreline, open water, or back roads. Keep the geography with the memory.

Illustration · Blue Mesa Reservoir

Optional GPS route tracking

Turn on route tracking when you want a record of where you traveled during a trip. Leave it off when you do not. It is there when the day calls for it.

Use it walking a river, wading, fishing from shore, kayaking, canoeing, trolling, running a boat, or working your way between nearby spots.

The route belongs
to the story.

Record it from the trip screen

Route recording sits on the trip screen, right under Log Catch. Pause it while you move to the next spot. Stop it when you are done. When one place is all you need, Save Exact Spot keeps just that.

Spots and routes stay private. They are saved in your journal, not posted anywhere.

See catches in context

A fish is easier to remember when you can see where it happened. Catch locations can sit right on the route, so the trip reads as a morning that moved rather than a list of times.

Keep places connected to trips

A saved spot is more useful when you know which days happened there. Places stay tied to the trips around them, so a pin on the map comes with its own history.

Look back at the route, not just the destination

Years later, a line on a map brings back details that a place name alone cannot. The bend in the river. The shoreline you walked. The stretch where you kept stopping. The path you took across the lake before the wind came up.

That movement is part of the day too.

Maps become part of your history

Routes and catch locations do not end when the trip does. They turn up again in your trip recaps, your fishing history, your yearly recap, and the photo books you make from a season.

In a photo book, the waters you fished share one map, each with its trips, fish, and months. The pins mark the general location of the water, not the spots you fished.
